A year of daily speaking practice: what actually changes

A year of daily practice can change how you speak, but nobody can promise a level by a date. Here is what actually changes, and what it takes.

Published September 10, 2023 · 9 min read · Sławomir Onyszko ·Updated November 8, 2026

Many promises about learning a language in a year start with a number and end with a level. They skip the only part that matters: what you do every day.

A year is a useful container for practice. It is not a guarantee. The result depends on where you start, which language you are learning, how often you practice, and whether the practice makes you produce the language or only recognize it.

I have been on both sides of that gap. I could read and understand a lot before I could speak. The first time I tried to say something in a real conversation, my head went quiet. The words were there, but they did not come out. What changed was not a hidden method. It was a daily loop that made me speak, corrected me, and brought the corrections back.

What a year is good for

A year gives you many small sessions. It gives you enough repetitions to build a habit, enough mistakes to see a pattern, and enough corrections to notice what you actually need to work on.

A year does not give you a level by itself. Two people can practice for a year and finish in very different places. One may speak in short sentences about familiar topics. Another may handle a work meeting. A third may still freeze. The difference is not talent. It is what they did in those sessions.

What happens in those minutes

Imagine two people with the same 15 minutes a day.

The first person opens an app, picks the right answer from four options, keeps a streak, and feels productive. The second person says a sentence out loud, gets a correction, writes down what went wrong, and reviews the correction a few days later.

After a year, the first person has practiced recognition. The second person has practiced production. Recognition helps you understand. Production helps you speak. They are different skills.

You can recognize a song after two chords. Singing it is a different job. Language works the same way. Knowing the word is not the same as building a sentence with it under mild pressure.

Three things that turn practice into speaking

You produce the language

Production means you build your own sentence and say or write it. Not choose it from a list. Not recognize it. Build it.

In Spanish, you might want to say "I am 30 years old." If you translate from English, you may say "Soy 30 años." The natural version is "Tengo 30 años." The difference is small, but it is exactly the kind of thing that only shows up when you produce the sentence yourself.

Soliloquy asks you to answer speaking prompts, describe images, and handle everyday scenarios. You can also add your own tasks. The point is not to repeat a phrase. The point is to make your mouth and your brain do the work.

You get a correction you can understand

A correction is useful when it tells you three things: what you said, what you should have said, and why.

"That was wrong" is not a correction. "Soy 30 años" is not wrong because you made a random mistake. It is wrong because Spanish uses "tener" for age, not "ser." Once you see that, you can fix the pattern, not just the sentence.

Soliloquy records your answer, transcribes it, shows the corrected version, and explains the errors. Every correction can become a flashcard, and all your corrections collect in one error diary. That diary is your personal list of things to watch.

The correction comes back at the right time

You will forget things. That is normal. The question is whether something brings them back before they disappear.

Spaced repetition is a simple idea. You review a word or a correction at the moment you are about to forget it. If it is easy, it comes back later. If it is hard, it comes back sooner. It works like a friend who asks you the same question a few days later, just before you would have forgotten it.

In Soliloquy, words from stories, corrections from speaking, and phrases you practice all become cards in one deck. You do not manage decks or schedules. The app decides what is due.

What a daily session looks like

A typical session is 10 to 15 minutes. You open the app and see what is due: a story, a speaking task, new words, and flashcards.

You read a short story at your level and on topics you chose. You answer a speaking prompt and get a correction. You learn a few words by writing your own sentences with them. You review the cards the system picked for today.

There is no appointment, no audience, and no need to summon courage for a video call. You can do it alone, at home, on an ordinary evening.

The daily goal can be set from 5 to 60 minutes. The default session is short on purpose. A small session you repeat is more useful than a heroic session you do once and abandon.

What changes early, and what changes later

The first changes are usually small. You freeze less. You can say a sentence without stopping in the middle. You start noticing your own mistakes. You remember a correction from last week.

Later, the sentences get longer. You can handle a conversation with more ease. You can explain an idea, tell a story, or handle a problem. Your pronunciation becomes easier to understand.

What nobody can promise is a level by a date. A B2 certificate in a year, a fluent conversation in three months, a native accent: those are not plans. They are hopes with a date attached.

Accent is part of who you are. The goal is not to sound like someone else. The goal is to be understood without extra effort from the person listening.

What a year cannot do

A year of daily practice cannot replace real conversation. A tutor or a patient friend is still the best place to practice spontaneity, interruptions, jokes, and the messy parts of a real conversation. A good tutor is the gold standard.

A year of daily practice can give you the foundation that makes those conversations possible. It can make you less afraid to start. It can give you the sentences and the corrections you need to keep going.

It cannot remove your accent, and it should not try. It cannot guarantee a certificate, and it should not pretend to. It cannot do the work for you. It can make the work easier to repeat.

How to judge progress without a streak

A streak is a nudge. It is not a grade. It tells you that you showed up. It does not tell you that you spoke.

Better signs of progress:

  • You can say more sentences about your day than you could a month ago.
  • You understand a correction the first time you see it.
  • You remember a word from a story without looking it up.
  • You can handle a speaking task that used to feel hard.
  • You can hear the difference between what you said and what you meant to say.

These are small, concrete signs. They are more useful than a number that only counts taps.

If you miss a few days

You will miss days. A plan that only works when everything goes perfectly is not a plan.

When you come back, the app shows what is due and what to review first. Your progress is saved. You do not start from zero. You restart the loop.

The goal is not a perfect streak. The goal is a practice you can return to.

How to start without a big plan

You do not need a one-year plan, a stack of books, or a perfect schedule. You need one small loop you can repeat.

  1. Pick a language you actually want to use.
  2. Set a daily goal you can keep, even on a busy day.
  3. Read something at your level.
  4. Say something out loud and get a correction.
  5. Review what you learned before it disappears.

Soliloquy sets this up in 2 to 3 minutes. You choose your language, level, motivation, and topics. Then today's practice is ready.

Hard questions

Can I reach B2 in a year?

No one can promise that. It depends on your starting point, the language, how much you practice, and what you do in that practice. A daily loop gives you a real chance to improve. A date on a calendar does not.

Do I need a tutor?

A tutor is the best place to practice real conversation. Soliloquy is not a replacement for that. It is a way to practice speaking, get corrections, and review them every day, so you can bring more to the conversations you have with a person.

What if I miss a week?

You restart. Your progress and your corrections are still there. The app shows what to review first. Missing a week is not a failure. It is a week.

A year is enough to build the habit

A year will not guarantee a level. It is enough time to build a daily practice, collect a record of your mistakes, and see what changes when you speak instead of only recognizing.
